lines: Pairing is one press now. The browser's list opens, the rider picks the bike, and Telo Ride connects to it.
Only the press opens the list, and it asks for Echelon's service or FTMS. Under the button, a hint about the Echelon app.
If the rider closes the list, nothing goes wrong. If a policy blocks it, an alert says so, with Try again.
The card reads the name the bike advertises, so an Echelon EX-5s shows its model and its own identifier.
Pairing subscribes first, then writes three commands to start the bike, one at a time, at least three hundred milliseconds apart.
The button turns busy with a spinner. On the bike's first notification, the card gets its check, and Home opens.
Other smart bikes speak FTMS. Telo Ride reads their data and range, and sets resistance only once the bike grants control.
The bike is remembered. Next time, Telo Ride opens on Home and reconnects to it, without the list.
Still to come: keepalive and automatic reconnects in the next slice, then the read only status and the signal strength.
Pairing looks the same on a phone, a tablet, a laptop or a desktop.
What the tests prove: twenty-five behaviour specs and sixty-two unit tests, all green.
Telo Ride, from the Telo family, turns a smart bike at home into a game.
It pairs with the bike over Bluetooth, reads your power and sets resistance for every hill and interval.

lines.text: Two doors: Race, ride a map against your best-time ghost, bots or people; and Classes, ride along to a video, alone or with a group; fed by one progression of XP, rider levels, stars and map unlocks.
